fields.h1: Build a School Climate Survey for Students, Staff, and Families
fields.hero_description: Build a school climate survey that stores no student names and saves every answer with its grade and role.
fields.features_heading: What Each School Climate Survey Includes
fields.features_subheading: Six things Emergent builds from one description of your school and the groups you plan to ask.
fields.feature_1:
Questions drafted from your goals

Describe your grades and groups and what the results should change. Emergent drafts statements on safety and on ties with adults and peers, and you reword any of them with a prompt.
fields.feature_2:
No names or student IDs kept

Each answer is saved with a grade or role and nothing else. Ask for a survey with no login and no student ID field, and say on the first screen what the survey keeps and why.
fields.feature_3:
A version for each group

Build versions for students, staff, and families in one prompt, with shared statements worded alike. Emergent sets no cap on responses, and every answer lands in a database you own.
fields.feature_4:
Every question broken out by group

See agreement on every question by group and by term. Set a minimum group size, and any group under it stays out of the report instead of showing a few people on their own.
fields.feature_5:
Low results sent to their owner

Pick a line for each topic and the person who owns it, like the counselor for safety. When a question falls under its line, that owner gets a Slack or email alert naming the group.
fields.feature_6:
Your district domain, your code

Host the survey on the district domain, included with Emergent and paid in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and run it again next year.

fields.usecase_heading: What Each Group's Answers Turned Up
fields.tab_content_1:
Hallway safety flagged in one grade

Students in grades 6 to 8 answer the survey anonymously during advisory. Each question is scored as the share of students who agree, and any question under 60% agree in a grade goes to the counseling team. In grade 7, 61 of 127 students agreed with "I feel safe in the hallways between classes."
fields.tab_content_2:
Staff answers kept to the role, never the name

Teachers and support staff open the staff survey from a link, and the survey keeps only their role. Any role with fewer than 5 answers is held back from the report, which kept the 3 administrators' answers out of it. The principal sees what remains: 16 of 38 teachers agree that they have a say in decisions.
fields.tab_content_3:
One school's drop caught across six

A district office runs one climate survey in all 6 of its schools, and each school gets a safety score out of 100. Harbor View Middle fell to 64 against 78 a year earlier, a 14-point drop, while no other school moved more than 3 points. Its principal got the score with the questions behind it.
fields.tab_content_4:
Advisory tested by a spring rerun

Each fall and again in spring, a high school asks the same questions in the same words. After the fall results, it added a weekly advisory period for grade 9. In spring, 280 of 412 students in grade 9 agreed with "An adult at this school knows me," against 213 of 410 in the fall.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a School Climate Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a school climate survey whose results lead to changes students and staff can see.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Name the decisions on the table
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set a time and a window
fields.howto_step_1_des: List the choices the results could settle this year: where adults stand between classes, whether advisory stays, which grade gets a new program. Every item should inform one of them. Start your prompt with that list, and Emergent writes the items to match.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Decide which grades and staff roles take part, and whether families do. Ask each group only what it sees firsthand. A parent can rate how welcome they feel at pickup but not how a class runs, and a student can rate a hallway but not a hiring decision.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write each item as a plain statement with one idea, such as "Adults at this school treat me with respect," and use one agree scale for every item. For younger grades, keep statements under 12 words and avoid words like climate or engagement.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give students a set class period, such as advisory. Answers then come from the whole grade, not only from the students who check email. Leave the survey open for 2 weeks for staff and families, and send one reminder halfway through.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Run the survey with one class or a few staff volunteers first. Time how long it takes, ask which statements confused them, and open the table to confirm no name or ID came through with the answers. Reword anything they stumbled on.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Start with the gaps: a grade or a role well below the rest. Then read the open comments from that group. A schoolwide average can hide one grade that feels unsafe. Write down the two or three gaps you will work on first.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Share the changes, then ask again
fields.howto_step_7_des: Within a month of closing the survey, tell everyone who took part what the results showed and the one or two changes you will make. Repeat the survey next term without rewording it, and compare the two sets of answers.

faq_plan.q: What is a climate survey for school?
faq_plan.ref: What is a climate survey for school?

prov.original: What is a climate survey for school?

faq_plan.a: A school climate survey asks the people in a school how it feels to them: whether they feel safe there and connected to the adults and peers around them. Answers are read by group, such as a grade or a staff role, never by name. One federal version, EDSCLS, is a suite of survey instruments NCES developed for schools, districts, and states.

faq_plan.q: How do you design a student school climate survey?
faq_plan.ref: how to design a student school climate survey
faq_plan.a: Start with the decisions the results should inform, then write short statements students rate on one agree scale. Group them by topic, such as safety or belonging. Keep it under 15 minutes and give it during a class period. Emergent's AI survey builder drafts the statements from your description, stores each answer with a grade only, and charts the results grade by grade.

faq_plan.q: What is the purpose of a school climate survey?
faq_plan.ref: What is the purpose of a school climate survey?

prov.original: What is the purpose of a school climate survey?

faq_plan.a: The purpose is to find the groups where students and staff feel unsafe or unheard and to aim changes there. A grade that avoids one hallway or a staff role that feels left out of decisions shows up as a gap against the rest. Run it again each year and the same questions show whether the changes worked.

faq_plan.q: Can a private school run its own school climate survey?
faq_plan.ref: how many states use school climate surveys
faq_plan.a: Yes. A private or parish school can write and run its own, with the same rated statements on safety and belonging a public school uses. Send it apart from any church survey the parish runs. Students then rate school life, and families answer about the classroom, not the congregation. Pick topics your board can act on this year.

faq_plan.q: Why are school climate surveys important?
faq_plan.ref: why are school climate surveys important
faq_plan.a: They turn what a school hears as stories into numbers by group: which grade feels unsafe, which staff role feels ignored. A principal can then aim one change at one gap and check it the next year. Emergent sets no response cap, and a district can survey every student and staff member at once.

faq_plan.q: What are good school climate survey questions?
faq_plan.a: Good school climate survey questions are short statements rated on an agree scale. Students might rate "Adults here care about how I am doing" on that scale. A fairness item could read "Rules are enforced the same way for everyone" in place of a broad question on discipline. Staff get their own statements on support and on having a say in decisions.

faq_plan.q: How often should you run a school climate survey?
faq_plan.a: Once or twice a school year, in the same weeks and with the same wording each time. A fall round finds the gaps, and a spring rerun shows whether the changes reached them. A customer feedback survey can follow every order. A climate survey sent every month leaves no time for a change to show up in the answers.
faq_plan.note: B-w-215 2026-10-16: AlsoAsked "Are school climate surveys anonymous?" (locked, PA6 yes/no flag) rejected by Divit; slot converted to a written question (precedent: service-request-form slot 4)

faq_plan.q: What topics should a school climate survey cover?
faq_plan.a: Most cover three areas, and the federal EDSCLS names them: engagement, safety, and environment. Its questionnaires for students and staff cover 3 domains and 13 topics. Pick the topics tied to a decision your school can make this year, such as hallway supervision or advisory, and save the rest for a later round.
faq_plan.note: B-w-215 2026-10-16: flagged Semrush question rejected by Divit; replaced with a written question

faq_plan.q: How do you share school climate survey results with families?
faq_plan.a: Send a short note from the principal that pairs each finding with the change it led to, such as more adults in the hallways after a low safety score. Report by grade, never by class, and leave out any group too small to keep its answers anonymous. Emergent can build the results page on your district domain, with charts drawn from answers in a database the district owns.
faq_plan.note: B-w-215 2026-10-16: flagged Semrush question rejected by Divit; replaced with a written question

faq_plan.q: How do you build a separate school climate survey for staff?
faq_plan.a: Give staff their own version, with statements about their work such as support from leaders and a say in decisions. Word a few items exactly as in the student version to compare the two views. The federal EDSCLS keeps separate questionnaires for students, instructional staff, and non-teaching staff and principals. Staff on their way out get an exit survey instead.

plan.angle: The top 10 is the instruments themselves: state surveys (Georgia, Virginia, Nevada, California), the federal EDSCLS suite, PBIS Apps, PERTS and research centers. Each explains one fixed survey; none shows a school or district how to run its own and act on the results. This page answers the informational intent in the FAQ (what it is, purpose, private schools, questions, anonymity, rating scale, analysis, who takes it), with no state-specific programs and then shows four school climate surveys built from a prompt: an anonymous student survey that flags a low item by grade, a staff survey that hides small role groups, a district view that catches one school's drop, and a fall and spring pair that shows whether a change worked. The student-survey and parent-survey siblings own those primaries; this page owns climate across every group.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a School Climate Survey for Students, Staff, and Families'; hero 'Build a school climate survey that stores no student names and saves every answer with its grade and role.' (107 chars); how-to description is one sentence of 104 chars.

intent.evidence: AMBER angle carried: the FAQ answers the informational intent with sourced state and federal instruments (EDSCLS, Nevada, CHKS, Delaware 31 questions / seven domains), and the tabs and how-to show a school running and acting on its own survey.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: advisory period, counseling team, grade 7 hallway item, minimum role size of 5, district safety score out of 100, fall and spring rerun.

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: 'Students in grades 6 to 8 answer the survey anonymously during advisory.', 'Describe your grades and groups...', 'List the choices the results could settle this year...'.

craft.evidence: No tacked-on endings; Q2 and Q5 clean; sentences carry one idea ('Start with the gaps: a grade or a role well below the rest.').

voice.evidence: Plain, product-led copy ('Any role with fewer than 5 answers is held back from the report'); forced link analogies in FAQ 4, 7, 10 kept as a note.

truth.evidence: Every third-party fact sits inside its quoted span (EDSCLS 'suite of survey instruments', Nevada 'each fall', CHKS 'school climate', Delaware 'thirty-one questions ... seven domains'); Emergent lines map to prompt-build, database-owned, alerts, no-caps, code-export, custom-domain; numbers agree across copy, alt and images (61/127=48%, 78-64=14, 213/410=52%, 280/412=68%).

distinct.evidence: Owns climate across every group (district view, staff role minimum, fall/spring rerun); no student survey or parent survey primary in a heading.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions, each answered in its first sentence; hub link in item 2; links to church survey, customer feedback survey, exit survey; locked items 1, 3, 7 verbatim; no brand or file format in a question.

images.evidence: Contact sheet: one hero per tab; grade 7 '61 of 127 agree, 48%' under 'Under 60%'; '16 of 38 teachers agree' with 'Administrators hidden, 3 answers'; Harbor View '78 last year, down 14 points' and no other school past +3; '68% agree in spring' vs '52% in the fall'. Every image matches its tab copy.
